meta.title: Resource-Efficient Super-Resolution for Multispectral Data: a Progressive Focused Transformer Approach

abstract: The increasing demand for high-resolution multispectral imagery has highlighted the limitations of current satellite platforms, where spatial resolution remains constrained by hardware and downlink bandwidth. In this paper, we propose a lightweight super-resolution method designed for onboard deployment, capable of enhancing Sentinel-2 four-band RGBNIR multispectral data while preserving spectral integrity. Our approach leverages a Progressive Focused Transformer (PFT) architecture, optimized for computational efficiency, that is adapted for 4× super-resolution of four-band RGBNIR Sentinel-2 imagery. Operating at 84.96 GFLOPs/MPix with only 792K parameters, our model achieves a Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM) of 5.08◦on a 100-tile RGBNIR benchmark, outperforming SEN2SR-M — the current spectral state of the art — at 3× lower computational cost, without any post-hoc spectral correction. Unlike hybrid approaches that enforce spectral consistency through post-hoc constraints, the PFT learns inter-band coherence intrinsically through its progressive attention mechanism. These results suggest the potential of Transformer-based SR for onboard Earth observation pipelines.

blocks.html: Onboard artificial intelligence is reshaping Earth observation: ESA’s Φ-sat-1 demonstrated that deep neural networks can run directly on spaceborne hardware, opening a new paradigm where data is processed before downlink rather than after. Onboard processing is particularly valuable when the downlink is the limiting factor, rather than the sensor. Applications such as wildfire and flood detection benefit from products generated before transmission, since only the relevant subset of data needs to be sent to ground, reducing latency in time-critical scenarios [1, 2]. In this context, enhancing spatial resolution directly on-board allows downstream detection and delineation tasks to operate on finer spatial detail without increasing the volume of transmitted data. Yet the spatial resolution of spaceborne sensors remains fundamentally constrained by sensor physics, orbital altitude, and downlink bandwidth. Although Sentinel-2 offers a 10 m ground sampling distance for visible and near-infrared (NIR) bands, many operational applications including infrastructure monitoring, precision agriculture and change detection would greatly benefit from higher spatial detail.

blocks.html: In this work we restrict the analysis to the four native 10 m bands (B2, B3, B4, B8): they are the only Sentinel- 2 bands acquired at the finest available ground sampling distance and they are required to compute widely used spectral indices such as NDVI. This four-band RGBNIR configuration is moreover representative of the payloads carried by many smallsat and cubesat missions, which provide only visible and near-infrared channels [3].

Super-Resolution (SR) offers a software path to close this gap without hardware upgrades. Deep Learning has revolutionized image super-resolution: initially, CNN based methods [4, 5] replaced classical interpolation, followed by GAN-based methods [6] able to produce sharper outputs at the cost of spectral hallucinations [7]. However, for multispectral satellite data, visual sharpness is not sufficient. Quantitative downstream analysis relies upon radiometrically accurate pixel values. Spectral indices such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) [8] are highly sensitive to inter-band distortion.

The trade-off between visual quality and spectral fidelity is a central problem when designing a super-resolution method for multispectral images [9]. The literature has converged on two strategies for managing this issue: (1) adversarial training with explicit radiometric consistency constraints [10], which improves spectral fidelity but increases architectural complexity, and (2) post-hoc correction frameworks, such as Fourier-domain constraints applied after SR inference, which decouple spectral accuracy from the core learning objective. SEN2SR-M [7] represents the current state of the art in spectral accuracy through a hybrid architecture incorporating Fourier-domain spectral constraints during inference. Both approaches treat spectral integrity as an external constraint rather than a property that emerges naturally from the model’s optimization.

In this work, we propose to follow a different strategy and adapt the Progressive Focused Transformer (PFT) [11], an architecture originally designed for RGB Super-Resolution, to natively process four-channel RGB- NIR multispectral data. By training the model end-to-end with a uniform L1 loss across all spectral bands, we empirically found that inter-band correlations can be learned intrinsically, without explicit spectral supervision. Furthermore, at 84.96 GFLOPs/MPix, the PFT is a possible candidate for onboard integration on modern edge AI hardware.

Transformer-based architectures have shown that global self-attention can capture long-range spatial dependencies that convolutional filters cannot effectively model, yielding significant gains on standard benchmarks [12]. The PFT model [11] extends this line by introducing Progressive Focused Attention (see Fig.1). This mechanism inherits attention maps from previous layers to progressively refine them, achieving strong performance at substantially reduced computational cost than dense-attention Transformers. We will show that an end-to-end Transformer can intrinsically learn inter-band coherence—eliminating the need for post-hoc consistency corrections—while operating at 3× lower computational cost than SEN2SR-M (84.96 vs. 266.4 GFLOPs/MPix). This efficiency makes the approach practical for onboard embedded deployment.

In this Section, we present the method proposed to design a resource-efficient super-resolution methodology for multispectral data. It leverages Progressive Focused Transformer (PFT) [11], that operates through a series of attention blocks which process local input feature windows in a sequential manner. The key innovation is the Progressive Focused Attention (PFA): previous layers contribute to the calculation of current layer’s attention by using the Hadamard product. This operation progressively sparsifies the attention map providing an exponential reduction in computation while amplifying only the most relevant tokens, as shown in Figure 1.

The original PFT accepts a 3-channel RGB input. We made two targeted architectural modifications for 4-channel RGBNIR processing. First, the initial convolutional layer (conv_first) and the final pixel-shuffle reconstruction layer were extended to accept and output 4 channels respectively, enabling simultaneous processing of all spectral bands within a single forward pass. This forces the attention layers to learn cross-channel dependencies rather than treating each band independently.

Second, we trained the network entirely from random initialization rather than fine-tuning from RGB-pretrained weights. NIR reflectance characteristics differ fundamentally from visible-spectrum bands — vegetation exhibits high NIR reflectance precisely because of cellular structure, not pigmentation — so RGB-pretrained features would introduce a systematic spectral bias. Random initialization ensures the network treats all spectral bands equally from the beginning.
We employ a pixel-wise L1 loss applied uniformly across all four spectral bands:

blocks.html: where C = 4, H = W = 256. The equal weighting across bands is a deliberate design choice: it prevents the optimizer from sacrificing NIR accuracy to minimize loss on the three visible bands. L1 is preferred over L2 for its robustness to outliers and its empirically sharper reconstructions. Perceptual and adversarial losses are excluded as they are known to introduce spectral distortions [7].

The model was trained using the Adam optimizer with base learning rate 2 × 10−4, a 10k-iteration linear warmup, and MultiStepLR decay (γ = 0.5) at iterations {150k, 225k, 270k, 290k}, totaling 300k iterations with batch size 32. Exponential Moving Average (EMA, decay 0.999) of model weights was maintained during training and used for inference. The implementation is built on the BasicSR framework [13].

Our dataset consists of Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery restricted to the four native 10 m bands: B2 (Blue), B3 (Green), B4 (Red), and B8 (NIR). The training set comprises 5,000 image pairs and the validation uses 100 held-out pairs. Ground truth patches are 256 × 256 × 4 crops from full-resolution Sentinel-2 tiles. Low-quality inputs are generated by bicubic downsampling by a factor of 4, yielding 64 × 64 × 4 inputs, following the Wald protocol [15]. The dataset spans diverse land cover types including urban environments, agricultural fields, forest areas, and mixed rural scenes, ensuring the model encounters varied spectral and structural conditions during training. Standard geometric augmentations (random horizontal/vertical flips, 90° rotations) are applied during training. Reflectance values are handled in the [0, 1] range for both the low-quality inputs and the ground truth. The training and validation splits are disjoint. No hyperparameter search was performed: the training schedule follows the configuration of the original PFT work [11]. The 100 held-out pairs are used exclusively for the final evaluation reported in Table 1.

blocks.html: We assess reconstruction quality with two complementary indices. The Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), reported in degrees, measures the average angle between the spectral vector of each reconstructed pixel and that of the corresponding reference pixel: it quantifies inter-band angular distortion independently of overall intensity, and is therefore the quantity that directly determines the reliability of band-ratio products such as NDVI. blocks.html: Table 1 presents our results against a Bicubic interpolation baseline and SEN2SR-M, evaluated on our 100-tile Sentinel-2 RGBNIR validation set. The PFT-light achieves SAM of 5.08◦, outperforming SEN2SR-M on the RGBNIR protocol (7.10◦) despite its 3× lower FLOPs number (84.96 vs. 266.4 GFLOPs/MPix) and 17× fewer parameters (792K vs. 13.8M). The ERGAS index of 5.82 confirms globally consistent radiometric quality. The result is methodologically significant: SEN2SR-M applies an explicit Fourier-domain spectral constraint post-hoc — PFT-light achieves superior RGBNIR spectral fidelity through end-to-end learning alone.

Table 2 reports per-channel PSNR and SSIM across three geographically distinct test scenarios. A consistent pattern emerges: visible bands (R, G, B) achieve higher reconstruction accuracy than NIR, a finding likely caused by the limited representation of NIR-specific textures<sup>1</sup> in the training set and the fundamentally different spatial statistics of NIR reflectance in vegetated areas. The urban scenario (Bitonto) shows more uniform performance across bands, as artificial surfaces exhibit more correlated spectral signatures [16]. This per-band analysis guides future work: NIR-specific data augmentation and band-adaptive loss weighting could be promising directions to close the visible-NIR performance gap.

blocks.html: Figure 3 presents visual comparisons (LQ input, GT reference, SR output) for the RGB composite and NIR channel across all three test scenarios. The PFT reconstructs sharp boundaries between land cover classes — field edges, road networks, building footprints — that are entirely absent in the bicubic baseline. Furthermore, vegetation areas exhibit consistent NIR enhancement without the chromatic hallucinations typical of adversarially-trained models, where false spectral structure is introduced to satisfy a discriminator. The NIR channel retains spatial texture that is physically coherent with the RGB bands, as reflected by the consistent SSIM scores across channels within each scenario (Table 2).

Spectral integrity in the super-resolved data. The consequences of spectral distortion are better illustrated through a concrete example. NDVI [8] is the most widely used index for vegetation monitoring, computed directly from the ratio of NIR and Red band reflectances. Adversarially trained models are known to introduce spectral hallucinations [7] — inter-band angular distortions that shift pixel NDVI values by amounts sufficient to reclassify pixels across standard land-cover thresholds. The PFT’s SAM of 5.08◦, compared to 7.25◦for bicubic interpolation, demonstrates a substantial reduction in spectral distortion that preserves the scientific utility of derived products, making super-resolved imagery effective for Earth observation analysis, not just visually appealing.

End-to-end spectral learning vs. post-hoc correction. SEN2SR-M’s Fourier-domain constraint achieves spectral accuracy by replacing the low-frequency components of the SR output with those of the original LR input after the network’s prediction. This is effective but it treats the neural network as a spatial upsampler and the Fourier constraint as a spectral corrector, decoupling two properties that are physically entangled in multispectral data. The approach based on PFT, which learns spectral coherence through progressive self-attention over 4-channel inputs, demonstrates that end-to-end learning can improve the spectral fidelity of correction-based methods at lower total computational cost, without requiring spectral domain expertise to be encoded as an explicit constraint. This has practical implications for model portability: a selfcontained neural network with no post-processing steps is far easier to deploy in onboard inference pipelines (Table 1).

Computational feasibility for onboard deployment. At 84.96 GFLOPs/MPix, the PFT operates well within the computational budget of modern edge AI hardware. For reference, the Intel Myriad X VPU (used in ESA’s Φ-sat-1 mission [1]) delivers approximately 4 TOPS of inference throughput while modern edge platforms like The NVIDIA Jetson Orin module provide up to 275 TOPS [17]. Even accounting for memory bandwidth constraints, inference on a single 64 × 64 × 4 input tile is achievable in tens of milliseconds on such hardware. A self-contained network with no post-processing steps is moreover far easier to validate and deploy in edge inference pipelines than a twostage hybrid system. Limitations and future directions. The current evaluation is limited to 5,000 training pairs, a single sensor (Sentinel-2), and four spectral bands (RGBNIR). The quantitative comparison reported in Table 1 is based on a validation set comprising 100 tiles, which necessarily limits the statistical resolution available for assessing small performance differences. Expanding the held-out dataset would enable a more robust evaluation and yield tighter confidence intervals for the reported metrics. A second limitation concerns the adopted degradation model. Specifically, the low-quality inputs are generated using a purely geometric downsampling operator; consequently, the current evaluation does not fully characterize the method’s robustness to sensor noise, optical blur, atmospheric variability, or other acquisition-related artifacts encountered in real-world imagery. Future work will therefore assess the proposed method using more realistic degradation pipelines and investigate its robustness when the degradation operators used during training and testing are mismatched.

It would also be important to extend to larger datasets, additional sensors such as Landsat-8/9 or PlanetScope, and the full Sentinel-2 spectral range (13 bands) in order to validate the generality of the approach. Architecturally, incorporating spectral cross-attention — attention computed across the channel dimension rather than the spatial dimension — could explicitly model inter-band relationships and further reduce SAM without requiring post-hoc corrections. A direct extension is the incorporation of a spectral angle loss term during training: minimizing

as an auxiliary objective alongside L1 would explicitly penalize inter-band angular distortion, potentially reducing SAM below the 5.08◦achieved with uniform L1 supervision alone. Finally, extending beyond 4× SR to 8× or 10× upsampling would open the possibility of generating Sentinel-2-like imagery from sensors with coarser spatial resolution.
